label: Chapter 1: A Settlement in the Marsh

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So, mud. Walk me through it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The river is called the Senne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And you have to imagine it nothing like a proper river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a small, slow stream that used to wander across a wide, wet valley, splitting into channels, making little islands as it went.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Not exactly a glamorous start.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not at all. But people had been living around the edges of that valley for a very long time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There are traces of Iron Age settlers at a site called Champ Saint-Anne, in the neighborhood of Anderlecht.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I'm going to guess the Romans showed up, because the Romans always show up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did, sort of. Roman farms and country houses were scattered across the countryside.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But no real Roman town on the spot.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Huh. I'd have bet money on a Roman town.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'd have lost. After the empire faded, Frankish settlers moved in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in that same field in Anderlecht, they've found a Frankish cemetery with more than three hundred graves, from roughly the years five hundred to seven hundred.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Three hundred graves. So that's not a passing visit.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No. That's farmers and fighters living in small villages on the dry ground above the river, inside the new Frankish kingdom, the one that eventually grows into Charlemagne's empire.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. I can feel a legend coming.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You're right. There's a legend.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Go on.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Tradition says that around the year five eighty, a holy man named Gaugericus, who's known in French as Saint Géry, the bishop of Cambrai, built a little chapel on an island in the Senne.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Is that true?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Honestly? Historians are cautious.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The sources are later and a bit shaky.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it's a good candidate for the seed of the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And here's the nice part. You can still go there.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's called Place Saint-Géry, in the old center, and there's an old market hall close to where the island used to be.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So what about the name? Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Earliest forms look something like Bruocsella.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And most scholars read that as a home in the marsh.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Or a dwelling by the swamp.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, that's honest.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's what a farmer would call a wet bit of ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it tells you something true.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This was a place that had to deal with water.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But hang on. If it's a swamp, why would anyone build a town there?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Good question. Geography. The Senne valley sat on an important route.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Trade roads ran from the cloth-making cities of Flanders in the west, to Cologne and the Rhine in the east.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Merchants went through carrying wool, cloth, wine, metalwork.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And they needed somewhere to stop.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly. A place to cross the river, or bring boats upstream.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the islands gave them safe ground.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the hills?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The hills to the east were a good place for a fortress.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, so it's a market town waiting to happen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Waiting to happen, yes. But for a long time it's still small, in a much bigger political world.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the ninth century, Charlemagne's empire is split up among his heirs.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: As happens.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As always happens. And the region that becomes Belgium gets caught in the middle, in a long contested territory called Lotharingia, named for the Frankish king Lothar.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It bounces back and forth between the western and eastern halves of the old empire.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who's actually in charge, though?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: On the ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not the dukes, really. They ruled Lotharingia on behalf of the German emperors, but they kept a loose grip.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So the local lords hold most of the real power.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right. So when do we get a proper date?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Late tenth century. In the year nine seventy-seven, the German emperor Otto the Second gives the duchy of Lower Lotharingia, which is roughly Belgium and part of the Netherlands, to a man called Charles.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who's Charles?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A member of the old Carolingian family.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A son of one French king and a brother of the next one.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Basically an exile from the throne of France, hunting for a power base.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, so he needs a castle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He needs a castle. And within a couple of years, he builds a fortification on one of the islands in the Senne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The same island as the old chapel.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Is that the founding?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Hold on, because something else matters even more.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In about the year nine seventy-nine, Charles moves the relics of a saint named Gudula, a pious woman from the seventh century, to the chapel on the island.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Gudula!

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You know her.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I love Gudula. Is it true that she went to church before dawn carrying a lantern?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. And the devil kept blowing out her light.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Every time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every time. And every time, an angel lit it again.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I like the angel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Everyone likes the angel. Anyway, Gudula becomes the patron saint of Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And that move of her relics is the date most often given as the official founding of the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But I sense a caution.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Always. Modern historians point out that the story of Charles building a castle and founding the city rests on sources written long afterwards.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The real picture is probably messier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A growing settlement, a chapel, a market, local lords, all developing over several generations.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it's not like somebody cut a ribbon.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Nobody cut a ribbon. But nine seventy-nine is the date that stuck.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the relics moved again, didn't they?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did. In 1047, a powerful nobleman named Lambert the Second, Count of Leuven, which is a city about twenty-five kilometers to the east, moves them to a new church on a hill overlooking the valley.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he sets up a college of priests there, called canons, to look after it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait, so that's the cathedral?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the ancestor of the cathedral.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The hill church was dedicated to Saint Michael, and in time to Saint Gudula too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it grows into the twin-towered cathedral you can still see today.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Saint Michael is the dragon slayer.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He is. He becomes the other patron saint of the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he ends up standing on top of the town hall, which we'll get to.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, so by now the pieces are in place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They are. Lowland market settlement on the river, with merchants and craftsmen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A church on the hill, with money and influence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A castle for protection. And the counts of Leuven, who increasingly see this place as an important part of their growing territory.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What about walls?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Around the year eleven hundred, the people build their first defensive wall.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Nothing grand, a modest circuit around the main settlement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Inside, maybe a few thousand people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They make cloth, bake bread, brew beer, trade.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A few thousand. So not a great city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Not yet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not yet. But a real town now. Walls, a market, a church, a lord.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it's about to take off.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. Next time, the counts become dukes, and the craftsmen start flexing their muscles.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that muddy market square...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Begins turning into one of the most famous squares in the world.
